 Learn more The odds are short that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month. Really, really short. So much so that it'd be surprising if the central bank doesn't tighten rates by at least 25 basis points before the end of this year. 
 In all likelihood, that isn't music to investors' ears if they're considering or already holding utility stocks -- a sector highly (and famously) correlated with interest rates.

 Here's the skinny on why utility equities are often viewed as vulnerable to rising rates. The sector is often prized by investors who are seeking above-average dividend yields with reduced risk. The problem is that when Treasury yields are high, as they are today, lower-risk government bonds look more attractive than high-dividend stocks, including supposedly low-volatility utilities. 
 These two utility stocks are ideal for risk-tolerant investors. Image source: Getty Images. 
 Add to that, the utility sector is capital-intensive and home to scores of companies with elevated debt burdens, so when rates rise, financing costs rise too, which can weigh on earnings. 
 Still, for investors who can stomach a bit of risk, some utility names may be worth examining even if rates rise. That group includes Hawaiian Electric Industries (NYSE:HE) and Portland General Electric (NYSE:POR). 
 Say Aloha to risk/reward 
 Rare are the occasions on which a utility stock is described as "risky," but that is the case with Hawaiian Electric Industries. This sub-$10 stock is down 27% year-to-date, and it's the unusual example of a utility stock that doesn't pay a dividend. Yikes! 
 As with some of its peers in California, Hawaiian Electric's shares have been hurt by wildfire liabilities. In this case, it was the 2023 Maui wildfires that saddled the company with significant financial obligations, so this is by no means the quintessential sleepy utility stock. 
 On the other hand, this utility may be on the road to redemption. The company has an agreement in place to settle wildfire claims for nearly $2 billion, and recently passed legislation in Hawaii grants utility regulators the authority to establish liability caps in the future. 
 For what it's worth, and it may be worth something to the adventurous souls out there, Morningstar has a $12 fair value estimate on this utility stock, implying upside of more than 33% from the Nov. 11 closing price. 
 Story Continues Interesting history and a decent dividend 
 For fans of market history, Portland General Electric is an interesting story because Enron once owned it. Yes, that Enron. In fact, when ownership of the utility was transferred away from Enron in April 2006, some of its equity was used to compensate Enron creditors. 
 Fast-forward to the here and now: This stock is down 4% year-to-date, but it yields 4.7%. The payout has steadily risen every year since 2006. 
 One of the issues prospective investors need to monitor with this utility stock is the company's relationships with data center operators. Earlier this year, Oregon regulators gave Portland General the green light to raise rates on data centers by an average of 29%. It remains to be seen if those data center firms will simply "deal with it" or explore sourcing power from elsewhere. 
 The company is also pushing a nearly 4% rate hike on residential customers, and that's not playing well in the court of public opinion. 
 Still, this utility stock isn't a lost cause. The regulatory environment in Oregon isn't as hostile to utilities as in some other states, and the company has clear guidance on what's expected regarding clean energy and carbon-reducing investments. 
 Power demand in the region is expected to grow over the long term (Portland General also operates in neighboring Washington State), which could support modest yet dependable payout growth.
